title: The other summit season: BRICS and the SCO have spotted a gap
gist: Nick Bisley argues BRICS and the SCO have evolved from niche groupings into focal points for illiberal/authoritarian cooperation that are exploiting the legitimacy gap left by failing Western-built institutions. BRICS (half the world's population, 40% of GDP) aims to restructure the global order while the SCO stays security-focused; Southeast Asian states are increasingly engaging both, which Australia must track.

insights.claim: BRICS and the SCO have become focal points for cooperation among illiberal and authoritarian states, and their recent expansions are part of a broader trend of such powers cooperating to advance their interests.
insights.speaker: Nick Bisley
insights.so_what: Signals a consolidating alternative institutional bloc that can reshape trade, finance and sanctions regimes.
insights.quote: The recent expansion of the groupings is part of a larger trend in which illiberal and authoritarian powers are increasingly cooperating to advance their interests.
insights.locator: The recent expansion of the groupings

insights.claim: Expanded BRICS, beyond Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, now includes Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Indonesia and the UAE, and represents half the world's population and 40% of global GDP.
insights.speaker: Nick Bisley
insights.so_what: Scale gives BRICS critical mass to push alternatives to Bretton Woods-era structures.
insights.quote: Representing half the world’s population and 40% of global GDP, the body has critical mass.

insights.claim: The SCO has ten members including Russia, China, Iran and India plus 17 observer and partner states such as Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, Cambodia and Egypt, and is one of few groupings recognising Myanmar's junta.
insights.speaker: Nick Bisley
insights.so_what: The SCO offers diplomatic cover to pariah regimes, affecting sanctions efficacy.

insights.claim: These groupings are expanding because they sense an opportunity in the failings of existing North Atlantic-built institutions, whose criticisms as unrepresentative and dysfunctional are real; the West has been slow to notice this 'gap in the institutional market'.
insights.speaker: Nick Bisley
insights.so_what: Western institutional decay is a structural tailwind for alternative financial and governance architectures.
insights.quote: BRICS and the SCO have spotted a gap in the institutional market. The West has been slow to notice.
insights.locator: The recent expansion of the groupings

insights.claim: For much of their history both groupings had limited ambitions: the SCO focused on Central Asian border security and counter-terrorism, while BRICS settled for a 'relatively meagre' development bank in 2014 despite seeking major global economic reform.
insights.speaker: Nick Bisley
insights.so_what: A track record of underdelivery tempers expectations for near-term BRICS financial architecture.
insights.quote: While BRICS sought major reforms of the global economic order, it had to settle for the creation of a relatively meagre new development bank in 2014.
insights.locator: The SCO is more than a quarter-century

insights.claim: The SCO is geopolitically ambitious but its output on international order has been little more than grand rhetoric, remaining focused on Central Asian and Eurasian security.
insights.speaker: Nick Bisley
insights.so_what: SCO headlines should be discounted as market-moving events.
insights.quote: While it has issued broad-ranging statements about international order and globalisation, there has been little of substance beyond grand rhetoric.

insights.claim: BRICS's New Delhi Declaration ran to nearly 45 pages covering UN reform, restructuring of the Bretton Woods Institutions and even new university ranking systems, reflecting an ambition to restructure international order around the Global South.
insights.speaker: Nick Bisley
insights.so_what: Watch BRICS for IMF/World Bank reform pressure and alternative financial standards.

insights.claim: Southeast Asian states, once uninterested, are now engaging BRICS and the SCO: Indonesia joined BRICS; Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam attended the 2026 summit; Myanmar and Laos became SCO dialogue partners.
insights.speaker: Nick Bisley
insights.so_what: ASEAN alignment is diversifying, affecting Western influence and trade-bloc bets in the region.
insights.locator: For Australia, a further development is of note.

insights.claim: The trend reflects Southeast Asian states looking beyond ASEAN for influence and advantage, which need not cost ASEAN but which Australia must understand as the global order shifts.
insights.speaker: Nick Bisley
insights.so_what: Australia's regional strategy and partner reliability assumptions face erosion.
